5zqM2YoHJ7s.title: When to Sell Stocks Never Answer With a Price
5zqM2YoHJ7s.desc:
Knowing when to sell stocks seems simple: pick a price and wait for it. Yet bitcoin ETFs made 8.5% a year, while the average dollar people put in them lost almost 6% a year.

In this video I dig into Morningstar's study of nearly 23,000 US funds to see if this only happens in crypto. We start with the usual rule that index funds are investing and coins are speculating. But the "boring pile" leaks too: over ten years the funds made 9.9% a year, and the average dollar got 8.7%. "Smaller hole, same hole."

Then we get to the one question that tells investing from speculation, no matter what you own: when would you sell? We also cover why checking your app every morning sets you up for panic selling, who gets paid when you trade, and why a red screen is really "a sale" while you're still buying.

Finally, how bitcoin ETFs rose while the money in them fell, and the one line to write in your notes app before your next dollar goes anywhere. Finish it with a date or a reason. Never a price.

0:46 The Boring Pile Leaks Too
1:35 Investing Or Speculating?
2:05 Why Checking Daily Hurts
2:44 Who Profits When You Trade

3:49 Buying High, Selling Low

6w1Slz0Cddo.title: $10,000 at Chase Earns $1 a Year
6w1Slz0Cddo.desc:
A Chase savings account feels like the safe place for your money. Then you check the interest rate: 0.01%, or just $1 a year on $10,000, while the average credit card charges about 21%.

In this video I line up the savings accounts at America's four biggest banks against six years of price data. We start with the advice your parents swore by, spend less than you make and bank the rest, and why it's good advice. The catch? Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo all pay 0.01%, so ten years on $10,000 earns you "one lunch, no drink."

Then we go deeper into the real damage: what inflation does to your savings. Put $10,000 in that account in January 2020, and today you're about $2,300 poorer for doing everything right. Even a high-yield savings account at around 4% mostly just keeps pace after tax. We also cover how banks make money with your savings, and why nobody's rushing to warn you.

Finally, why saving money is still worth it, but where it lives matters. I'll show you a 10-second check to tell if your savings is growing or quietly shrinking, and where to put your savings instead. That $1 isn't really interest. It's a tip for staying put.

thB17K7AbYs.title: Too Many Interests That’s Where the Money Is
thB17K7AbYs.desc:
If you have too many interests, everyone says pick one: one skill, 10,000 hours, no side projects. But the money shows up when two of your interests touch.

In this video I look at four studies on learning, creativity, jobs and hiring to find out why Disney handed its animation studio to a computer scientist in 2006. We start with the generalist vs specialist question: picking one thing wins in what psychologist Robin Hogarth called a "kind" environment, but your job, money and business are "wicked."

Then we look at why that advice is a risky bet. An MIT team found that about 6 in 10 American workers in 2018 had job titles that didn't even exist in 1940. We also cover who "pick one" was really built for, and why one skill means one kind of buyer, which makes you "easy to sort, and cheap to keep."

Finally, why multiple interests are a sign of high openness to experience, not a character problem, and how Disney's new boss combined two of his own interests and helped start Pixar. That's also a simple way to start making money from your hobbies: find one buyer for two of your interests at once. Not a business plan. Just one name.

V3oBkgzghnw.title: If You're Building a Business in Your 20s, Watch This
V3oBkgzghnw.desc:
Starting a business in your 20s can feel like a race you're already losing. But the fastest-growing new companies in America, the top one in a thousand, are started by founders who are 45 on average.

In this video I go through a study of 2.7 million founders to find out why, and what to do in your 20s if you feel late. We start with why feeling behind in your 20s makes sense, and what this decade really gives you: not time, not energy, but "cheap mistakes." At 23, losing $400 on phone cases nobody buys stings for a week. At 40, the same mistake costs $40,000 of your family's savings.

Then we go deeper into why a mistake is only cheap if you learn from it, and why nobody tells you to slow down: urgency sells, and "your fear is somebody else's business model." We also cover the real edge that 45-year-old founder has, knowing one industry from the inside, and why your 9-to-5 isn't what's stopping your business. It's the lab where you'll find it.

Finally, a simple way to find a business idea this week: write down every problem people at work complain about more than once, then ask the person stuck with it one question. Your 20s aren't the race. They're the research.

eUJ2X8L1vcg.title: Why $100K Earners Still Live Paycheck to Paycheck
eUJ2X8L1vcg.desc:
Most people think living paycheck to paycheck is an income problem, so they chase a bigger salary. But nearly half of Americans earning over $100K still live that way, because the number that matters was never your salary.

In this video I go through a year of my own bank statements to find the number your salary hides. We start with cash flow vs income: income tells you how much arrives, cash flow tells you where it goes and when. What's left after every payment you've already promised is your real salary, your "free cash flow."

Then we look at why almost everything is priced to hide that number, from "only 49 a month" to a burrito split into four payments. We also cover why ending a $400 car payment can beat a $400 raise, and how small payments that run the other way, like a rented parking spot or savings that earn interest, turn your personal cash flow around.

Finally, how people end up living paycheck to paycheck on six figures, and the one thing to do this week if you want to stop: measure your free cash flow. It was never an earning problem. It was a direction problem.

0:36 Income Is The Wrong Number
1:39 Priced To Hide It
